U.S. Central Command says American forces disabled a commercial bulk carrier in the Gulf of Oman on Thursday after its crew allegedly tried to run the U.S. naval blockade against Iran.

According to CENTCOM, a U.S. military aircraft launched precision munitions that struck the stern of the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer after the ship departed the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas and ignored multiple warnings. The vessel's propulsion was disabled, and CENTCOM says the civilian crew was unharmed.

U.S. forces say they have redirected 158 compliant commercial ships and disabled six vessels that refused to follow blockade orders. Meanwhile, tensions around the Strait of Hormuz continue disrupting global shipping and energy flows.

Can naval blockades and maritime pressure force a diplomatic shift with Tehran, or are shipping lanes heading toward wider escalation?

#CENTCOM #GulfOfOman #StraitOfHormuz

A Nazi commandant ordered him to hand over the Jewish American POWs.
Master Sgt. Roddie Edmonds replied: “We are all Jews here.”

In January 1945, Master Sgt. Roddie Edmonds was the highest-ranking American noncommissioned officer at a German POW camp.

A Nazi commandant demanded that all Jewish American prisoners step forward.
Edmonds ordered every man in the barracks to stand instead.

When the commandant pressed him, Edmonds said, “We are all Jews here.”

The officer put a pistol to Edmonds’ head and demanded he identify the Jewish soldiers.
Edmonds refused.
He told him that if he shot, he would have to shoot all of them — and that he would be prosecuted for war crimes.

The commandant backed down.

Edmonds’ actions saved an estimated 200 Jewish American POWs.

He never sought recognition. The story only fully came to light decades later through the testimony of the men he protected.

Some stands are taken quietly, under a gun, and still change everything.

U.S. Special Operations pioneer and Raider legend, Major Jim Capers: Major Capers is the Marine Corps’ first African American special operator, a member of the inaugural class of the U.S. Special Operations Command’s Commando Hall of Honor, recipient of the Medal of Honor, a Silver Star, two Bronze Stars with “V” for valor, and three Purple Hearts.

Most notably, during his time in Vietnam, he was one of the most decorated Marines in Raider history. He became the first African American to command a Marine Reconnaissance company and to receive a battlefield commission.

"I cried in my car after seeing this."
A passerby at The Upper Room Church watched a state trooper pull in to pick up dinner for someone in need — and the church provided a meal for the trooper as well. A little while later, driving through town in the rain, that same witness spotted the trooper pulled over and sitting right on the cold, wet sidewalk beside the person, sharing the meal together.
He didn't just drop off a box of food and drive away. He sat down, kept them company, and made sure they didn't have to eat alone.
A warm meal helps for a night, but giving someone your time and making them feel seen is something else entirely.
#Kindness #Humanity #StateTrooper

August 01, 2009 - Army Sergeant Gregory Owens Jr., 24, of Garland, TX, died July 20, 2009 in Wardak Province, Afghanistan, of wounds suffered when an improvised explosive device detonated near their vehicle followed by an attack from enemy forces using small arms and rocket-propelled grenade fires.

On July 29th his remains were flown to Carswell NAS in Ft. Worth. His family was escorted by members of the Patriot Guard of Texas, off base as military and civilian personnel lined the streets in a respectful salute.

A viewing was held on the evening of the 30th. That night I met Mr. & Mrs. Owens and given permission to take a photos and video of the funeral to share with other grateful American citizens.

Approximately 300 friends, family and close associates came to celebrate Sgt Owens life. A diverse group of people, made proclamations, recounted their fondest memories of him, and spoke of his character. His younger brother delivered a moving eulogy. US Army representatives posthumously, awarded Sgt. Owens with a Bronze Star for valor and the Purple Heart for wounds sustained in battle. A Southern Baptist minister delivered a high energy sermon. A small choir gave beautiful performances of southern gospel music.

The U.S. Supreme Court is set to hear oral arguments December 2 in a blockbuster Second Amendment case that could decide whether states and cities can ban AR-15-style rifles (CNN, SCOTUSblog).

Reviewing challenges to bans in Cook County, Illinois, and Connecticut, the justices' ruling—expected by June 2027—could impact "assault weapons" prohibitions currently in place across 11 states, Washington, D.C., and several major cities (CT Mirror, Denver Gazette). Challengers backed by the Trump administration and 27 Republican attorneys general argue that AR-15s are ordinary rifles in "common use" owned by 16 to 26 million Americans and are protected under Heller, while Cook County, Connecticut, and gun-control advocates counter that the Constitution allows states to regulate unusually dangerous weapons linked to mass shootings (CNN, CT Mirror).

How do you think the Supreme Court should rule on state AR-15 bans?

#SupremeCourt #SecondAmendment

Robert Lewis Howard (July 11, 1939 – December 23, 2009) was a highly decorated United States Army Special Forces officer and Medal of Honor recipient of the Vietnam War.

He was wounded 14 times over 54 months of combat, was awarded the Medal of Honor, eight Purple Hearts, a Distinguished Service Cross, a Silver Star, and four Bronze Stars.

He was nominated for the Medal of Honor three separate times over a 13-month period but received lesser medals for the first two nominations, which were for actions performed in Cambodia, where the U.S. was fighting covertly. He received the Medal of Honor for his actions on November 16, 1967, in North Vietnam, his third nomination.

He retired from the US Army after 36 years of service as a full colonel, and the most highly decorated service member on active duty.

He died as a result of pancreatic cancer and was buried at Arlington National Cemetery on February 22, 2010.

At the time of his death he was the most decorated living Medal of Honor recipient.

CITATION: For conspicuous gallantry and intrepidity in action at the risk of his life above and beyond the call of duty. 1st Lt. Howard (then SFC) distinguished himself while serving as platoon sergeant of an American-Vietnamese platoon which was on a mission to rescue a missing American soldier in enemy controlled territory in the Republic of Vietnam. The platoon had left its helicopter landing zone and was moving out on its mission when it was attacked by an estimated 2-company force. During the initial engagement, 1st Lt. Howard was wounded and his weapon destroyed by a grenade explosion. 1st Lt. Howard saw his platoon leader had been wounded seriously and was exposed to fire. Although unable to walk and weaponless, 1st Lt. Howard unhesitatingly crawled through a hail of fire to retrieve his wounded leader. As 1st Lt. Howard was administering first aid and removing the officer's equipment, an enemy bullet struck 1 of the ammunition pouches on the lieutenant's belt, detonating several magazines of ammunition. 1st Lt. Howard momentarily sought cover and then, realizing that he must rejoin the platoon, which had been disorganized by the enemy attack, he again began dragging the seriously wounded officer toward the platoon area. Through his outstanding example of indomitable courage and bravery, 1st Lt. Howard was able to rally the platoon into an organized defense force. With complete disregard for his safety, 1st Lt. Howard crawled from position to position, administering first aid to the wounded, giving encouragement to the defenders, and directing their fire on the encircling enemy. For 3 1⁄2 hours, 1st Lt. Howard's small force and supporting aircraft successfully repulsed enemy attacks and finally were in sufficient control to permit the landing of rescue helicopters. 1st Lt. Howard personally supervised the loading of his men and did not leave the bullet-swept landing zone until all were aboard safely. 1st Lt. Howard's gallantry in action, his complete devotion to the welfare of his men at the risk of his life, were in keeping with the highest traditions of the military service and reflect great credit on himself, his unit, and the U.S. Army.

Hackers have breached Cloud One, the U.S. Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform used to run military operations, logistics, maintenance, and personnel systems (TNW, Seeking Alpha).
According to sources cited by Reuters on November 27, U.S. Cyber Command has been called in to assess the damage after the intrusion disrupted internal workflows—pausing back-office application migrations, blocking updates to Cloud One apps, and stripping some users of administrator rights (Seeking Alpha, The Week). In a statement, the Air Force declined to discuss specific system vulnerabilities, saying it continuously takes prudent measures to protect department information and mission capabilities (Channel NewsAsia).

How vulnerable is U.S. military infrastructure when core operations rely on commercial cloud platforms?
#USAirForce #CyberSecurity

From running a mortar tube in shorts to gearing up in full plate carriers and rifles, U.S. special operators have long proved that Crocs in sport mode get the job done downrange.

FBI-TRAINED BOMB TECH & PBSO DETECTIVE ALAN SMITH KILLED BY WRONG-WAY DRIVER ON THANKSGIVING

Early Thanksgiving morning, Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office Detective Alan Smith was fatally struck by a wrong-way driver traveling southbound on I-95 (CBS Miami, Boca Post).

Alan joined PBSO in January 2007, became a Bomb Squad technician in 2012, graduated from the FBI Hazardous Devices School in September 2013, and served as an ATF Task Force Officer specializing in explosives investigations (CBS Miami). Outside of law enforcement, he was a college professor completing his doctoral degree, a loving husband to his wife, Jennifer, and a devoted father to his 14-year-old son, Alexander (CBS Miami).

Florida Highway Patrol troopers and PBSO deputies later arrested 37-year-old Raul Jonathan Espinoza Martinez at St. Mary's Medical Center—placing him in the same handcuffs Detective Smith carried—on charges including vehicular homicide and DUI manslaughter (CBS Miami).

Please keep Jennifer, Alexander, and the entire Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office in your thoughts and prayers.

#EndOfWatch #AlanSmith #PBSO

“By all reports and by the recording, they never stepped back. They never even shifted their weight. With their feet spread shoulder-width apart, they leaned into the danger, firing as fast as they could. They had only one second left to live, and I think they knew. The truck explodes. The camera goes blank. Two young men go to their God. Six seconds. Not enough time to think about their families, their country, their flag, or their lives or their deaths, but more than enough time for two very brave young men to do their duty. Those are the kind of people who are on watch all over the world tonight for you, and as amazing as this selfless act of sacrifice may seem, it is the norm.” ~ Gen. John Kelly

On Thanksgiving Day 2003, President George W. Bush pulled off one of the tightest secrets of his presidency—flying into Baghdad in the dark to become the first sitting U.S. president ever to visit Iraq (The Guardian, Al Jazeera).

While reporters were told he was spending the holiday at his ranch in Crawford, Texas, Bush slipped out Wednesday evening, switched planes at Andrews Air Force Base, and landed at Baghdad International Airport with cabin lights off and shades drawn (CNN, Medium). Wearing a 1st Armored Division Army jacket, he emerged from behind a curtain at the Bob Hope Dining Facility to surprise 600 soldiers, joking "I was just looking for a warm meal somewhere" before serving turkey and taking photos for roughly two and a half hours (White House Archives, PBS NewsHour, Al Jazeera).

Were you deployed or remember watching this surprise visit in 2003?

#Thanksgiving2003 #GeorgeWBush

President Donald Trump laughed off claims that the White House is pushing for a Russia-Ukraine peace deal by January, asking "Who said that?" and "He wants me to do what?" (Ukrainska Pravda).

In a New York Post interview reported November 25, Trump said he is not under a timeline and noted "it takes two to tango," adding that both Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Vladimir Putin shift from day to day on whether they are ready to settle (Hromadske). A day earlier, Zelenskyy told Bloomberg that U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff want a settlement as soon as possible, ideally by January, while cautioning that Ukraine wants peace "but not at Ukraine's expense alone" (European Pravda).

Do you think a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine is realistic by January, or is this war heading deeper into 2027?

The President of the United States of America takes pride in presenting the Navy Cross (Posthumously) to Petty Officer First Class (SEAL) Nicolas D. Checque, United States Navy, for extraordinary heroism while serving as a Hostage Rescue Force Team Member for a Joint Task Force on 8 December 2012 in Support of Operation ENDURING FREEDOM. The team infiltrated an enemy stronghold to rescue an American hostage from a well-armed and determined Taliban guard force. After aerial surveillance reported an active guard on the target compound, Chief Petty Officer Checque skillfully maneuvered and led the primary assault force toward the target building. In the final steps of the assault, a guard in the courtyard identified the approaching rescue force, and darted into the building. Chief Petty Officer Checque instinctively pursued and engaged a guard who peered from a doorway. Realizing the Taliban guards had been alerted and the hostage’s life was in imminent danger, Chief Petty Officer Checque unhesitatingly sprinted to the door and made entry. He was engaged by the enemy at close range and mortally wounded, but his bravery and unhesitant commitment in pursuit of the target was pivotal in saving the American hostage and the ultimate success of the overall mission. By his undaunted courage, bold initiative, and complete dedication to duty, Chief Petty Officer Checque reflected the highest credit upon himself and the military service.

RAPICAULT, PATRICK MARC (KIA), SILVER STAR RECIPIENT

Citation: The President of the United States takes pride in presenting the Silver Star Medal (Posthumously) to Patrick Marc Rapicault, Captain, U.S. Marine Corps, for conspicuous gallantry and intrepidity in action against the enemy while serving as Company Commander, Weapons Company, Second Battalion, Fifth Marine Regiment, FIRST Marine Division, I Marine Expeditionary Force, U.S. Marine Corps Forces, Central Command, in support of Operation IRAQI FREEDOM, from 24 September to 15 November 2004. Captain Rapicault courageously led his Marines on the streets of Ar Ramadi, Iraq, through 50 firefights and 27 improvised explosive device ambushes. Always leading from the front, he directed the fire and maneuver of his company with complete disregard for his own personal safety. Despite being the first Marine in the Battalion wounded and his company suffering the heaviest casualties during daily street fighting, Captain Rapicault always displayed an infectious enthusiasm that motivated every Marine to fight hard and recover quickly from battle. On every mission, Captain Rapicault's intuitive and calm combat leadership ensured success on the battlefield, with limited damage to vehicles and friendly casualties. He gallantly gave his life in the cause of freedom. Captain Rapicault's bold leadership, courageous actions, and complete dedication to duty reflected great credit upon him and were in keeping with the highest traditions of the Marine Corps and the United States Naval Service.

Elon Musk announced early Thursday that "Every child in America will receive two SpaceX shares, one from the company and one from me personally" (Forbes).

SpaceX confirmed it will contribute one newly issued share of Class A common stock to every active Trump Account next month, while Musk will match it with a personal share in June 2027 once his lockup period ends (Business Insider, Forbes). Based on SpaceX's Wednesday closing price of $127.44 and roughly 72 million American children, the combined pledge is estimated at roughly $18 billion—the largest private contribution to the federal children's investment program so far (TNW, Anadolu Ajansı).

Would you hold those SpaceX shares until your child turns 18?

#ElonMusk #SpaceX #TrumpAccounts

November 2004 — Cpl. Robert Mitchell of Kilo Company, 3rd Battalion, 1st Marines, fixes his bayonet as his unit advances down a street in Fallujah during Operation Phantom Fury.

Launched on November 7, 2004, the Second Battle of Fallujah brought roughly 13,500 U.S., British, and Iraqi forces into block-by-block urban combat that military historians describe as the heaviest fighting Marines and Soldiers faced since Huế City in 1968 (Wikipedia, Preceden). Assigned to Regimental Combat Team 1, 3rd Battalion, 1st Marines fought through fortified alleyways and buildings under sustained mortar, sniper, and RPG fire over six weeks of operations (Rebel Seed Studio, Wikipedia).

Drop a comment if you served in Fallujah or know someone who was there with 3/1.

#USMC #Marines #Fallujah

Marine Gunnery Sgt. Jeffrey E. Bohr Jr., Silver Star Recipient

Died April 10, 2003 Serving During Operation Iraqi Freedom

39, of Ossian, Iowa; assigned to 1st Battalion, 5th Marine Regiment, Camp Pendleton, Calif.; killed April 10 in northern Baghdad while engaging enemy forces.

Growing up in the tiny farm town of Ossian, Iowa, Jeffrey Bohr was a quiet kid who liked horses, enjoyed hunting and fishing, and did a little calf roping.

Later, as an Army Ranger and then a Marine, he parachuted into Grenada, helped oust Panamanian dictator Manuel Noriega, served in the Gulf War and trained for urban combat by rappelling out of helicopters and learning to float with his hands and feet tied.

Bohr, 39, died April 10 in a seven-hour gun battle in front of a Baghdad mosque. His wife, Lori, also a native Iowan, learned of his death from Marine officials as she was driving from California to Iowa to visit their parents. The couple had no children.

“I was proud of Jeff his whole life,” said his father, Edward Bohr, who lives in Ossian. “He was part of an anti-terrorist group and went through intense training. They even sent him to Colorado to learn to ski. When he came home on leave, he’d get up early in the morning and run 10 miles.”

His brother, Richard, who is in the Army Reserves and is scheduled to deploy to the Persian Gulf in May, hopes to visit the spot where Bohr died and erect a plaque.

Before leaving for the Middle East, Jeffrey Bohr chastised his father for being skeptical about sending troops to Iraq. “He said, ‘You don’t know as much about it as I do. We need to go there.’ He was ready to go. He was doing what he was good at.”

Citation: The President of the United States takes pride in presenting the Silver Star Medal (Posthumously) to Jeffrey E. Bohr, Jr., Gunnery Sergeant, U.S. Marine Corps, for conspicuous gallantry and intrepidity in action against the enemy while serving as Company Gunnery Sergeant, Company A, First Battalion, Fifth Marine Regiment, Regimental Combat Team 5, FIRST Marine Division, I Marine Expeditionary Force in support of Operation IRAQI FREEDOM on 10 April 2003. With his company assigned the dangerous mission of seizing a presidential palace in Baghdad and concerned that logistical re-supply might be slow in reaching his comrades once they reached the objective, Gunnery Sergeant Bohr selflessly volunteered to move in his two soft- skinned vehicles with the company's main armored convoy. While moving through narrow streets toward the objective, the convoy took intense small arms and rocket propelled grenade fire. Throughout this movement, Gunnery Sergeant Bohr delivered accurate, effective fires on the enemy while encouraging his Marines and supplying critical information to his company commander. When the lead vehicles of the convoy reached a dead end and were subjected to enemy fire, Gunnery Sergeant Bohr continued to boldly engage the enemy while calmly maneuvering his Marines to safety. Upon learning of a wounded Marine in a forward vehicle, Gunnery Sergeant Bohr immediately coordinated medical treatment and evacuation. Moving to the position of the injured Marine, Gunnery Sergeant Bohr continued to lay down a high volume of suppressive fire, while simultaneously guiding the medical evacuation vehicle, until he was mortally wounded by enemy fire. By his bold leadership, wise judgment, and complete dedication to duty, Gunnery Sergeant Bohr reflected great credit upon himself and upheld the highest traditions of the Marine Corps and the United States Naval Service.

A 33-year-old Georgia man faces a murder charge after authorities say he shot and killed his wife following an argument about Christmas gifts for their four children (Law & Crime).

The Walker County Sheriff’s Office said deputies called to a Rossville home were guided by a child to a bedroom, where Gene Allen was performing CPR on 32-year-old Bonnie Allen. She died from a gunshot wound to the head, according to reports. Investigators say the shooting came after a dispute over holiday presents. Allen was arrested and booked into the Walker County Jail six days later (The Mary Sue, Discover Walker, US Magazine).

Thinking of Bonnie Allen’s four children as they navigate this heartbreaking loss.

#Georgia #TrueCrime #CrimeNews

More than 240 retired U.S. F-15C/D Eagles are sitting in storage in the Arizona desert as the Air Force replaces them with F-35s and F-15EXs, while Ukraine waits years for new fighter deliveries (Forbes, Kyiv Post).

In a November 23 Forbes op-ed, retired U.S. Air Force Lt. Gen. David Deptula argued the Pentagon should assess refurbishing and transferring 50 to 60 of those retired Eagles to shoot down Russian drones and cruise missiles, freeing Ukraine's F-16s for other missions (Forbes). Deptula pointed out that production backlogs push large European deliveries of new F-16s, Gripens, and Rafales past 2028, though analysts caution that introducing another fighter platform would still require White House approval, spare parts pipelines, and more than a year of pilot and ground-crew training (Kyiv Post, Aerospace Global News).

Should the U.S. refurbish retired Arizona F-15s for Ukraine, or keep them in reserve?

#F15 #USAF #Ukraine

Carl Spurlin Dekel, a U.S. Marine who recently turned 100, shared his thoughts about what Marines and soldiers fought for during World War II. Dekel, who earned the Silver Star for bravery, said serving his country during the war was the most important thing he ever did. He would do it all over again. However, he feels upset about how things have changed over time. 💔

"People don’t realize what we did for them, it feels like it's all been forgotten."

He added, "The country I grew up in isn’t the same anymore. Today’s generation won’t have the same opportunities I had. It’s different now, and I don’t think it’s what the soldiers fought for."

Poland has asked NATO allies to consider shooting down Russian missiles over Ukraine when they are headed toward alliance territory (Kyiv Post).

The push follows a November 20 barrage in which three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles crashed in southeastern Poland, followed by another Russian drone entering Polish airspace earlier this week (Kyiv Post, PAP). Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said intercepting incoming threats over Ukraine at Kyiv's request constitutes self-defense, while Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk announced plans for a no-fly zone along Poland's eastern border so pilots can engage targets using radar and allied intelligence (Kyiv Independent).

Supporters of earlier interceptions say waiting until missiles cross the border leaves too little reaction time and puts civilians at risk, while cautious NATO allies warn that firing into Ukrainian airspace could pull the alliance into direct conflict with Russia (Kyiv Post, New Voice of Ukraine).

Should NATO intercept Russian missiles over Ukraine, or keep defenses strictly inside alliance borders?

#Poland #NATO #Ukraine #Russia

As a female military police officer, US Army Staff Sergeant Katteri Franklin had a much different experience than her fellow male Soldiers while serving in Iraq.

"The Iraqi women would stare at me and I would ask them what they were looking at," reflected Franklin. Their response would be that they had never seen a woman in uniform before."

Despite their initial curiosity and sometimes shock, the Iraqi women learned to trust Franklin and consider her an ally. She was able to use her gender to her advantage by helping them be more comfortable around U.S. servicemembers.

"The Iraqi women would seek me out when they needed medical or aid supplies, "said Franklin."They felt more comfortable around me."

Due to Franklin's willingness to interact closely with the Iraqi civilians, she became a critical part of ensuring that the local women and children had access to aid and medical treatment during her mission. Franklin's service in Iraq earned her a Bronze Star.

"I think it was easier for them to talk to me because I was a female," said Franklin, who was one of 22 female Soldiers in her Company and one of five in the Platoon.

In addition to building relationships with the women civilians, Franklin was a team leader in training the Iraqi police. She led up to 11 U.S. Soldiers at a time when they would go outside the wire to the Iraqi police stations and teach security measures.

"I learned a lot about the Iraqi people that I didn't know before," reflected Franklin. "I also learned a lot about my Soldiers. They managed to do things I never thought they could before we left (the U.S.). It was humbling to lead such fine Soldiers."

Franklin and her Soldiers worked closely with interpreters to communicate with the Iraqi police and their families. One accomplishment that she is most proud of from her service in Iraq is the progress she could see through the Iraqi police.

"We got them to patrol in areas where they previously would not go because of former terrorist activity," said Franklin. "When the security on the ground changed, our other strategies began to take shape."

"We got them to patrol into areas where they previously would not go because of former terrorist activity," said Franklin. "When the security on the ground changed, our other strategies began to take shape."

After two deployments, one to Iraq, Franklin is currently finishing U.S. Army recruitment school in the U.S. She hopes to become an Army recruiter and eventually go to officer training school. She wants to lead Soldiers for the remainder of her career - even though Franklin herself only joined the Army because she passed Basic Training.

Two former Horry County, South Carolina police officers former Deputy Chief Brandon Strickland and former Sgt. Damon Vescovi were indicted on obstruction of justice and misconduct in office charges tied to the September 2023 fatal road-rage shooting of Scott Spivey (AP News / KVUE, WLTX).

The two men involved in the shooting, Weldon Boyd and Kenneth Bradley Williams, were initially cleared under South Carolina's Stand Your Ground law, but now face murder charges after Spivey's sister filed a civil lawsuit and uncovered new evidence (The Washington Post).

That evidence included Boyd's recorded phone calls and body-camera footage showing Vescovi writing a note at the scene that read "act like a victim camera" (The Washington Post).

What does this case say about the power of a family refusing to stop digging for answers?

In the face of danger, most would run toward safety. Yet, when then-Lance Cpl. Corbin was faced with such a decision, he ran toward peril and possible death – braving intense enemy fire to help injured comrades.

Corbin, a medium tactical vehicle replacement driver, and his unit were stationed in the Al Anbar province to help secure and stabilize the volatile area. They had just finished several days of routine patrol on May 7, 2005, and were returning to the Haditha Dam when they got the call.

A platoon from their battalion was under attack on the east side of the Euphrates River and needed support to block the insurgents' retreat. Corbin's team – a quick reaction force (QRF) – quickly responded to the call. As the QRF crept toward the attack site, there was an unnatural stillness in the air.

“There was no one out, nothing moving,” Corbin later told the Marine Corps Times.

With every nerve on alert, the QRF kept driving toward the ambush site, knowing there were injured Marines that needed them. Suddenly, a vehicle laden with IEDs sped toward the convoy and blew up between two of the Humvees. Another blast followed as enemy fighters began firing upon the group.

The swift attack devastated Corbin's team – three of the four vehicles were severely damaged, and 11 of 16 Marines were injured or killed. Taking control of the situation, Corbin immediately repositioned his vehicle between the insurgents' fire and the wounded Marines. As he radioed in the situation, he began directing a counter-attack.

As those that could return fire, Corbin began recovering dead and wounded personnel and moving them toward safety. Running through the line of fire, Corbin grabbed his wounded patrol leader and threw him over his shoulder. He then sprinted back to his Humvee, firing at enemies as he ran. Corbin ran back and forth several times through the kill zone, moving everyone he could out of the withering fire and loaded them into his vehicle.

Arming every able Marine with as much ammunition and weapons as they could hold, Corbin drove his severely damaged Humvee through the kill zone toward the battle aid station. Even injured, the Marines were a deadly force to be reckoned with. Insurgents continued to pelt the rumbling truck with mortars and small-arms fire, but the Marines made it to safety.

Corbin's quick actions ensured that no Marines were killed after that initial attack. For his leadership, Corbin was awarded the Navy Cross on April 12, 2006.

The Ultimate Stand: Gary Gordon And Randy Shughart At Super Six Four
The Radio Requests From Above On October 3, 1993, during the intense street fighting of the Battle of Mogadishu, Black Hawk helicopter Super Six Four, piloted by Chief Warrant Officer Michael Durant, was struck by an RPG and crashed into a hostile neighborhood. Circling overhead in Super Six Two, Delta Force sniper team leader Master Sgt. Gary Gordon and his partner Sgt. 1st Class Randy Shughart watched armed hostile crowds numbering in the thousands converge on the downed wreckage. With no ground rescue convoy capable of reaching the site in time, Gordon radioed command requesting permission to be inserted on foot to protect the wounded crew. Command denied the request twice, warning that two men could not survive against an entire armed city. On their third urgent request, knowing rescue was hours away, command relented and cleared them for insertion

Fierce Defense And The Final Weapon Infilled roughly 100 meters away, Gordon and Shughart fought their way through an intense maze of shanties under heavy fire to reach the wreckage. They pulled Durant, who had sustained a broken leg and crushed vertebrae, from the crushed cockpit alongside his crew, moving them behind the fuselage to establish a perimeter. Fighting with bolt-action sniper rifles and sidearms, both snipers held off waves of militia until their ammunition ran dry. After Shughart fell, Gordon salvaged a rifle with the remaining rounds, handed it to the injured pilot with the parting words, “Good luck,” and went back into the fight with only his sidearm until he was overwhelmed

First Medals Of Honor Since Vietnam The stand of Gordon and Shughart delayed the armed crowd long enough to keep Durant alive until he was taken prisoner and ultimately released 11 days later. On May 23, 1994, both snipers were posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor, becoming the first service members to receive the nation’s highest military decoration since the Vietnam War

At 32,000 feet over Pennsylvania, an ordinary Tuesday morning flight suddenly became every aviator’s worst nightmare.

A metal fatigue fracture inside the left CFM56 engine sheared off a fan blade at cruising speed. Within milliseconds, the entire cowling disintegrated into flying shrapnel, puncturing the fuselage and blowing out a cabin window at row 14.

The cockpit erupted into instant chaos. Rapid decompression roared through the airframe, dropping cabin temperature below zero, flooding the cockpit with white vapor, and filling the air with deafening wind noise. The Boeing 737 shuddered violently, banking hard to 41 degrees with only one operational engine and zero internal communication back to the flight attendants.

In command was Captain Tammie Jo Shults, backed by First Officer Darren Ellisor.

Decades before flying commercial routes, Shults was breaking barriers in naval aviation as one of the first women to pilot the supersonic F/A-18 Hornet and fly tactical profiles in the A-7 Corsair II. She had spent years mastering emergency procedures on pitching carrier decks in pitch darkness, conditioning her nervous system to replace fear with immediate muscle memory.

While cockpit alarms blared and the airframe fought severe aerodynamic drag, Shults keyed her microphone to Philadelphia air traffic control. Her voice did not crack. Her cadence did not waver. She sounded like someone ordering a morning coffee.

"Southwest 1380 has an engine fire," she transmitted calmly. "We would like to descend."

When the controller asked whether the aircraft was actively on fire, her reply was cold steel.

"No, it is not on fire, but part of it is missing. They say there is a hole and someone went out."

Wrestling asymmetric thrust and flap damage, Shults manually stabilized the crippled airliner, brought it down on runway 27L at 165 knots, and safely delivered 148 souls home.

When catastrophe strikes at 32,000 feet, how does military flight discipline prepare pilots for split-second commercial emergencies?

“WE SPENT 52 DAYS IN THE DMZ MEAT GRINDER. HALF MY COMPANY WAS KILLED OR WOUNDED BEFORE MY 18TH BIRTHDAY.” — Vietnam Marine Machine Gunner Johnnie Clark on The Shawn Ryan Show.

Combat Marine machine gunner and author Johnnie Clark shares harrowing recollections of surviving Operation Prairie in the demilitarized zone during the Vietnam War.

In his own words:

“I enlisted in the Marine Corps as a teenager and was immediately sent up north to the DMZ as an M60 machine gunner—the most dangerous job in the infantry.

We were thrown into Operation Prairie fighting the North Vietnamese Army in the jungle. For 52 straight days, we were under constant mortar barrages, sniper fire, and mass human-wave assaults.

You’re sleeping in muddy trenches filled with leeches and trench foot, covered in the blood of boys you went through bootcamp with.

In less than two months, over half my company was killed or wounded. I watched my squad leader take a round right through the chest while handing me ammunition.

When you survive that kind of unrelenting carnage at 18 years old, a piece of your youth dies in that jungle forever. You spend the rest of your life trying to justify why God chose you to walk off that hill when so many better men stayed behind.”

Georgia has officially moved to restrict female athletic divisions exclusively to biological females, barring transgender women from competing on all girls and women’s sports teams statewide.

The action mandates that athletic eligibility in state-sanctioned interscholastic sports be determined strictly by biological sex at birth, covering all public school athletics and collegiate divisions operating under state association guidelines.

The policy follows a widespread national campaign led by female athletes, parents, and advocates including former Kentucky collegiate swimmer Riley Gaines, who has spent years speaking out across state legislatures following the controversial 2022 NCAA championships. Advocates have argued that male puberty provides enduring physical advantages in strength, lung capacity, and bone density that compromise both athletic safety and competitive fairness for biological women.

The decision places Georgia alongside more than two dozen states that have enacted similar legal protections designed to preserve the original intent of Title IX in scholastic sports.

Supporters emphasize that creating protected categories for biological women is essential to ensuring female athletes continue to have equal access to podium finishes, championship titles, and athletic college scholarships. Meanwhile, opposing advocacy groups continue to challenge these state-level restrictions in federal court, arguing that policies restricting participation deny transgender students equal participation in school athletic programs.

As more states move to codify biological sex standards in female athletic divisions, how will these policies reshape the legal landscape of women’s sports nationwide?

In the face of danger, most would run toward safety. Yet, when then-Lance Cpl. Corbin was faced with such a decision, he ran toward peril and possible death – braving intense enemy fire to help injured comrades.

Corbin, a medium tactical vehicle replacement driver, and his unit were stationed in the Al Anbar province to help secure and stabilize the volatile area. They had just finished several days of routine patrol on May 7, 2005, and were returning to the Haditha Dam when they got the call.

A platoon from their battalion was under attack on the east side of the Euphrates River and needed support to block the insurgents' retreat. Corbin's team – a quick reaction force (QRF) – quickly responded to the call. As the QRF crept toward the attack site, there was an unnatural stillness in the air.

“There was no one out, nothing moving,” Corbin later told the Marine Corps Times.

With every nerve on alert, the QRF kept driving toward the ambush site, knowing there were injured Marines that needed them. Suddenly, a vehicle laden with IEDs sped toward the convoy and blew up between two of the Humvees. Another blast followed as enemy fighters began firing upon the group.

The swift attack devastated Corbin's team – three of the four vehicles were severely damaged, and 11 of 16 Marines were injured or killed. Taking control of the situation, Corbin immediately repositioned his vehicle between the insurgents' fire and the wounded Marines. As he radioed in the situation, he began directing a counter-attack.

As those that could return fire, Corbin began recovering dead and wounded personnel and moving them toward safety. Running through the line of fire, Corbin grabbed his wounded patrol leader and threw him over his shoulder. He then sprinted back to his Humvee, firing at enemies as he ran. Corbin ran back and forth several times through the kill zone, moving everyone he could out of the withering fire and loaded them into his vehicle.

Arming every able Marine with as much ammunition and weapons as they could hold, Corbin drove his severely damaged Humvee through the kill zone toward the battle aid station. Even injured, the Marines were a deadly force to be reckoned with. Insurgents continued to pelt the rumbling truck with mortars and small-arms fire, but the Marines made it to safety.

Corbin's quick actions ensured that no Marines were killed after that initial attack. For his leadership, Corbin was awarded the Navy Cross on April 12, 2006.

“I SERVED 14 YEARS. I GOT A PLAQUE WITH MY NAME MISSPELLED, AND A 15-YEAR PAYMENT PLAN.” — SEAL Team 6 Operator Matt Bissonnette on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most explosive interviews in the history of The Shawn Ryan Show (Episode #252), former DEVGRU assaulter Matt Bissonnette—who authored No Easy Day under the pen name "Mark Owen"—broke his 12-year silence on the raid that killed Osama bin Laden and the federal government's relentless legal retaliation against him.

In his own words:

“I’ve been fighting my own government for 12 years.

Three weeks after the Bin Laden mission, we go to Leon Panetta’s retirement ceremony in Langley, Virginia. He gets off stage and literally brings over Hollywood producers and directors, saying, ‘Hey look, they’re going to make you famous.’ They had full White House and CIA access to make Zero Dark Thirty.

I was an enlisted guy. I’m sitting there watching every single politician and leader from Washington talk about their heroic decisions for reelection campaigns, while none of the 24 operators who actually kicked the doors got any credit.

When I wrote No Easy Day, the government immediately came after me with unlimited attorneys. In the end, they admitted there was nothing classified in the book—they just wanted all the money back.

I spent $1.5 million of that money defending myself against their accusations. The government said, ‘We want that back too.’

So they put me on a garnishment plan: $3,800 every single month for the next 15 years. They told me if I miss one payment, they’ll charge me back taxes and prosecute me again.

I served this country for 14 straight combat tours. When I got out, I received a plaque with my first name misspelled—one ‘T’ in Matt. And now they want me paying them back for longer than I even wore the uniform.”

Washington politicians and intelligence officials handed classified access to Hollywood filmmakers for Zero Dark Thirty, yet when an enlisted SEAL who kicked the doors in Abbottabad wrote about his own experience, the federal government stripped every penny he earned and put him on a 15-year garnishment plan.

Gunnery Sgt. Aubrey McDade
1st Battalion, 8th Marines
Fallujah, Iraq, Nov. 11, 2004
Award: Navy Cross

Shortly after departing their base in Fallujah, then-Sgt. McDade and 1/8 Bravo Company's 1st Platoon entered an alley and encountered an immediate heavy volume of small arms and machine gun fire. In the opening seconds of the engagement, three Marines were seriously wounded as the well positioned and expecting enemy pinned others down. On contact, McDade rushed from the rear of the platoon column toward the kill zone and immediately deployed a machine gun team into the alley to provide suppressive fire on the enemy. After several attempts to reach casualties in the alley were met with heavy, well-aimed machine gun fire, he showed total disregard for his own safety by moving across the alley and successfully extracting the first of three wounded Marines from the kill zone. Aware of the fact that there were still two wounded Marines in the alley, McDade dashed through the heart of the kill zone two more times, each time braving intense enemy fire to successfully retrieve a Marine. After extracting the last casualty from the kill zone, he assisted in their treatment and medical evacuation. His quick thinking and aggressive actions were crucial in saving the lives of two of the three casualties.

“WE WERE EIGHT GUYS ON A ROOFTOP SURROUNDED BY THOUSANDS OF MILITIA FIRING THOUSANDS OF ROUNDS A MINUTE.”

On April 4, 2004, the holy city of Najaf, Iraq erupted into chaos as Muqtada al-Sadr’s Mahdi Army launched a coordinated uprising against coalition forces.

At the Coalition Provisional Authority (CPA) compound, a small detachment of eight Blackwater security contractors including former U.S. Marine Force Recon sniper Travis Haley found themselves cut off, outnumbered, and fighting for their lives against an advancing force of thousands.

Sitting down on The Shawn Ryan Show (SRS #172), Haley broke down the unvarnished reality of the legendary rooftop siege:

“The Mahdi Army had completely encircled the compound. We were on the roof eight guys with small arms and precision rifles looking out at hundreds, if not thousands, of armed insurgents advancing down the streets. You could literally hear the roar of the crowd before the firing started. When they opened up, the air filled with RPGs, mortars, and PKM rounds chewing up the parapet walls.”

“Brass was piling up past our ankles. I was on my precision rifle engaging targets one after another, working the bolt so fast that the barrel was smoking. At one point, I looked over at the guys next to me. We were out of ammunition resupplies, Spanish military forces inside had barricaded themselves below, and we knew if they breached the courtyard walls, we were going to be lynched and burned.”

“In that moment, fear disappears. You stop worrying about dying, lock your focus down to your optic, and decide that every single round left in your mags is taking an enemy down with you.”

Key takeaways from Haley’s breakdown of the battle:

The eight-man team manned the rooftop parapets for hours under non-stop direct fire, repelling wave after wave of militia assaults attempting to breach the perimeter gates.

With ammunition virtually exhausted and coalition ground reinforcements blocked, civilian Blackwater helicopter pilots braved intense anti-aircraft fire to hover directly over the embattled roof and kick out crates of 5.56mm and 7.62mm ammo.

The Warrior Mindset Under Siege: When survival looks impossible, combat psychology shifts from panic to cold, lethal execution—focusing strictly on fundamentals and making every pull of the trigger count.

The iconic footage of Haley working his precision rifle on that Najaf rooftop became one of the most widely watched combat videos of the early Iraq War.

On the morning of September 11, 2001, 34-year-old FDNY firefighter Stephen Siller had just completed a long shift with Brooklyn’s elite Squad 1 and was driving home to meet his brothers for a round of golf. When his emergency scanner announced that an airliner had struck the North Tower of the World Trade Center, Siller immediately turned his vehicle around and headed straight toward Manhattan.

Arriving at the entrance of the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel, Siller found it already barricaded and closed to all vehicular traffic for emergency security. Knowing his brother firefighters were already rushing into the burning towers across the river, Siller refused to turn back.

He strapped sixty pounds of heavy firefighting turnout gear onto his back, abandoned his vehicle at the entrance, and began sprinting on foot through nearly two miles of gridlocked subterranean darkness toward the financial district.

Emerging into lower Manhattan, Siller raced directly to the World Trade Center and entered the towers alongside fellow first responders to help evacuate thousands of civilians trapped on the upper floors. Siller gave his life that morning when the towers collapsed, leaving behind his wife and five young children. His legendary determination inspired his family to establish the Tunnel to Towers Foundation, an organization that has since provided debt-free homes and support to thousands of fallen first responder families, catastrophically injured service members, and Gold Star families nationwide.

What does Stephen Siller’s two-mile sprint through the darkness teach us about the true heart of a firefighter?
